original_value: Yellow rust, a widely known destructive wheat disease, affects wheat quality and causes large economic losses in wheat production. Hyperspectral remote sensing has shown potential for the detection of plant disease. This study aimed to analyze the spectral reflectance of the wheat canopy in the range of 350–1000 nm and to develop optimal spectral indices to detect yellow rust disease in wheat at different growth stages. The sensitive wavebands of healthy and infected wheat were located in the range 460–720 nm in the early-mid growth stage (from booting to anthesis), and in the ranges 568–709 nm and 725–1000 nm in the mid-late growth stage (from filling to milky ripeness), respectively. All possible three-band combinations over these sensitive wavebands were calculated as the forms of PRI (Photochemical Reflectance Index) and ARI (Anthocyanin Reflectance Index) at different growth stages and assessed to determine whether they could be used for estimating the severity of yellow rust disease. The optimal spectral index for estimating wheat infected by yellow rust disease was PRI (570, 525, 705) during the early-mid growth stage with R2 of 0.669, and ARI (860, 790, 750) during the mid-late growth stage with R2 of 0.888. Comparison of the proposed spectral indices with previously reported vegetation indices were able to satisfactorily discriminate wheat yellow rust. The classification accuracy for PRI (570, 525, 705) was 80.6% and the kappa coefficient was 0.61 in early-mid growth stage, and the classification accuracy for ARI (860, 790, 750) was 91.9% and the kappa coefficient was 0.75 in mid-late growth stage. The classification accuracy of the two indices reached 84.1% and 93.2% in the early-mid and mid-late growth stages in the validated dataset, respectively. We conclude that the three-band spectral indices PRI (570, 525, 705) and ARI (860, 790, 750) are optimal for monitoring yellow rust infection in these two growth stages, respectively. Our method is expected to provide a technical basis for wheat disease detection and prevention in the early-mid growth stage, and the estimation of yield losses in the mid-late growth stage.

result.paraphrase: Yellow rust, a well-known and highly destructive wheat disease, damages wheat quality and leads to substantial economic losses in wheat production. Hyperspectral remote sensing has demonstrated promise for plant disease detection. This study set out to examine wheat canopy spectral reflectance from 350–1000 nm and to develop the best spectral indices for detecting yellow rust in wheat at different growth stages. For healthy and diseased wheat, the sensitive wavebands were 460–720 nm in the early-mid growth stage (booting to anthesis) and 568–709 nm and 725–1000 nm in the mid-late growth stage (filling to milky ripeness), respectively. Using these sensitive wavebands, all possible three-band combinations were computed in PRI (Photochemical Reflectance Index) and ARI (Anthocyanin Reflectance Index) forms at different growth stages and evaluated to see whether they could estimate yellow rust severity. The best spectral index for wheat infected with yellow rust was PRI (570, 525, 705) in the early-mid growth stage, with R2 = 0.669, and ARI (860, 790, 750) in the mid-late growth stage, with R2 = 0.888. Compared with previously reported vegetation indices, the proposed spectral indices could satisfactorily distinguish wheat yellow rust. The classification accuracy of PRI (570, 525, 705) was 80.6% with a kappa coefficient of 0.61 in the early-mid growth stage, while ARI (860, 790, 750) achieved 91.9% accuracy with a kappa coefficient of 0.75 in the mid-late growth stage. In the validation dataset, the two indices reached classification accuracies of 84.1% and 93.2% in the early-mid and mid-late growth stages, respectively. We conclude that the three-band spectral indices PRI (570, 525, 705) and ARI (860, 790, 750) are optimal for monitoring yellow rust infection in these two growth stages, respectively. This method should provide a technical basis for early-mid-stage wheat disease detection and prevention, as well as yield-loss estimation in the mid-late growth stage.
